text.tspan: RF FRONT END — bought modules, SMA to SMA. Nothing here has a SPICE model at 2.4 GHz, so every one is measured on the bench, never simulated.
phone over its own AP, ch 1.
RF x LO. The carrier cancels and what is left is
a tone whose pitch is the range.
the ISM band off the LNA
Everything in the band above, written as a circuit SPICE can actually run. Build it first:
it shows you a beat tone before you have bought a single RF part.
Delay line, multiplier, then the amplifier's own filters. Bandwidth scaled down 10x and the
delay up 10x, because the carrier cancels: 4 MHz over 667 ns gives the same 417 Hz as 40 MHz
over 66.7 ns, and lets SPICE step at 10 ns instead of 20 ps.
1 VIDEO AMPLIFIER — 40 uV of audio in, line level out. Everything else on this sheet exists to feed it.
IF — -78 dBm at 417 Hz, which is 40 uV pk. This one wire carries the whole measurement.
Block 5 feeds the same wire the mixer does. That is the point of it:
you can bring up the whole amplifier, and see a 417 Hz tone come out of it,
with the RF half of the sheet still in its packaging.
Gain is 60.2 dB measured from the amplifier's own input, but 53.6 dB from the mixer, because 50 ohm driving 49.9 ohm halves the signal before the first stage.
The TX-to-RX leakage arrives alongside the echo at 8 mV and leaves at 27 mV. That 46 dB head start is what the two high-passes exist to cut down, and it is
why the gain is split in two: one stage of 1100 would saturate on the leakage long before the echo ever reached the output.
VANA powers all three op-amps here. VREF is their input reference: on a single supply every stage swings about 5.7 V, not about 0 V.
1N5822 makes a reversed plug harmless: VPROT reads -0.11 mV,
not -12 V. R15/C13 then filters the buck's 150 kHz to 4 mVpp.
VANA / 2, buffered, so the six returns inside block 1
VANA and VREF are net labels: every label with the same name is one wire.
VANA reaches block 2's divider and block 1's three op-amp rails.
VREF reaches six points inside block 1: R2, R4, R6, R8, C9 and the buffer.
4 SYNC DIVIDER — and the two channels the laptop actually records
Steps the PLL, holds SYNC high for the
up-chirp, turns the table between chirps.
so it cannot clip the input
SCK / MOSI / LE, each through 33 R, all the way back up to the PLL
Left channel is the measurement. Right channel is the clock: radar_acquire.py finds the chirp edges on it and derives T_up and the PRI
from them on every block, so changing the sweep on the ESP32 needs no matching change on the laptop.
ground_station/radar_acquire.py, once per block of 64 chirps:
read 48 kHz stereo -> find the sync edges (T_up, PRI) -> cut into 64 chirps
-> FFT along one chirp = RANGE -> FFT across the 64 = VELOCITY
-> CA-CFAR, peak-picked = DETECTIONS -> weight over azimuth = BEARING
-> {range, velocity, snr} to server.py, drawn in the browser.
Build and bench them in this order, because each needs the one before it:
3 first. Everything else runs on its output.
2 next. Block 1 will not bias without VREF.
1 then, driven at its IF pin by a signal generator.
4 whenever. It touches nothing else on the sheet.
5 any time, in SPICE alone, before the RF parts arrive.
